name: Jaw distraction after Rosenthal

lead: Jaw distraction after Rosenthal refers to the first documented use of distraction osteogenesis on the jaw, by the surgeon Wolfgang Rosenthal in 1930. In distraction, a cut bone is separated gradually so new bone forms in the gap, which in the face can lengthen a short or recessed mandible and change the profile.

The idea was not developed further for decades. It returned in the 1980s and a 1992 paper by Joseph McCarthy and colleagues described the modern clinical method for lengthening the human mandible, which is now used in craniofacial surgery.

paras: In modern practice the sequence is a surgical bone cut with a device attached, a roughly one-week rest, then gradual daily separation of the segments followed by a consolidation period and a second operation to remove the device. It is performed by craniofacial surgeons.

Reported complications of mandibular distraction include infection (about 5% in one summary), growth in an unintended direction, hardware failure, and injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, tooth buds or facial nerve.

angle.text: Gradual distraction can lengthen a short mandible, moving the chin forward and altering the side profile. It is a surgical option that craniofacial teams use for congenital and acquired jaw deficiency.

lead: Jaw distraction after Rosenthal is the name given in looksmaxxing and surgical-history discussion to the first recorded use of distraction osteogenesis in the jaw, attributed to Wolfgang Rosenthal in 1930.[1] Distraction osteogenesis is a surgical way to grow bone: a bone is cut, and the two segments are slowly pulled apart so that new bone forms between them.[1]

For appearance, its relevance is that the lower jaw can be lengthened or advanced this way, which changes chin projection and facial profile. Wikipedia reports that Rosenthal's jaw work was not pursued further until the 1980s, and that a 1992 paper by Joseph McCarthy and colleagues described the first modern clinical lengthening of the human mandible by gradual distraction.[1]
Today the technique is used mainly in craniofacial surgery for conditions such as hemifacial microsomia and micrognathia, and in infants with airway obstruction caused by a very small jaw.[1]

paras: Distraction osteogenesis proceeds in phases: an osteotomy (bone cut) with a device attached, a latency period of about seven days for early healing, an active distraction phase in which the device separates the segments, typically around 1 mm per day in two steps, and a consolidation period during which new bone hardens before the device is removed in a second operation.[1]
Separating too fast can lead to nonunion, where fibrous tissue forms instead of bone, while too slow a rate can allow the bone to fuse prematurely.[1]

Wikipedia traces the concept to a 1869 proposal by Bernhard von Langenbeck and a 1905 clinical report by Alessandro Codivilla, who treated 26 people with malformed legs and reported high complication rates.[1] Gavriil Ilizarov later developed external fixation and optimal separation rates after treating thousands of patients, which led to wide use in limbs.[1]

Rosenthal applied the principle to the jaw in 1930; the technique then lay largely unexplored until the 1980s, and McCarthy and colleagues published the modern mandibular lengthening report in 1992.[1]

A summary of mandibular distraction complications lists infection (about 5%), growth in an unintended direction (7-9%), hardware failure (3-4.5%), non-adherence to the distraction protocol (4.5%), inferior alveolar nerve damage (3.5%), tooth bud injury (2%) and facial nerve injury (0.5%).[1]

The craniofacial literature on mandibular distraction is substantial, but this article draws only on a general overview; the original 1930 Rosenthal case and the 1992 McCarthy report are described there rather than reviewed here.[1]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes the concept.[1]
Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempt, in the femur.[1]
Wolfgang Rosenthal performs the first jaw distraction.[1]
McCarthy and colleagues report modern clinical mandibular lengthening.[1]
